Bug_Title: Back references in regular expressions should only refer to capturing groups that are matched before the reference
Bug_Details:
When a back reference in a regex refers to a capturing group that hasn’t been defined yet (or at all), it can never be matched. Named back
references throw a PatternSyntaxException in that case; numeric back references fail silently when they can’t match, simply making the
match fail.
When the group is defined before the back reference but on a different control path (like in (.)|\1 for example), this also leads to a
situation where the back reference can never match.
Noncompliant code example
Pattern.compile("\\1(.)"); // Noncompliant, group 1 is defined after the back reference
Pattern.compile("(.)\\2"); // Noncompliant, group 2 isn't defined at all
Pattern.compile("(.)|\\1"); // Noncompliant, group 1 and the back reference are in different branches
Pattern.compile("(?<x>.)|\\k<x>"); // Noncompliant, group x and the back reference are in different branches
Compliant solution
Pattern.compile("(.)\\1");
Pattern.compile("(?<x>.)\\k<x>");
Bug_Explanation: The code contains four methods, each demonstrating a different aspect of the bug related to back references in regular expressions. In showBug1, the back reference \1 is used before the capturing group is defined. In showBug2, the back reference \2 refers to a capturing group that is not defined at all. In showBug3, the back reference \1 and the capturing group are in different branches of the regex. In showBug4, the named back reference \k<x> and the capturing group are in different branches of the regex.
Trigger_Explanation: The generated JUNIT test case triggers the bug by calling the methods showBug1, showBug2, showBug3, and showBug4 from the RegexBackReferenceBug class. Each method contains a regex pattern with back references that violate the rule of referring to capturing groups matched before the reference. The tests assert that the result is 'No match', which will fail if the regex pattern were to incorrectly match due to improper back referencing.
